Hi Samantha / Orion team,

Thanks again for the time yesterday. As promised, I pulled together an operational "journeymap" that ties the SKU decision (H100 vs A100 vs L4) to the three phases we discussed: initial reserve (predictable throughput), hybrid-burst (bursting into pooled capacity), and long-term hedge (mix for cost/availability).

High level:
- Memory-first workloads (large KV caches, long-context genomics ops) lean toward H100 reserve nodes because of 80GB+ GPU RAM and better FP8/TF32 perf for large models.
- Throughput and token-budget sensitive inference with shorter contexts are a good fit for L4 for steady-state cost efficiency; L4s are excellent for heavy batching and embedding pipelines.
- A100 is the pragmatic middle for mixed profiles and for customers who need consistent single-GPU performance and easier fallbacks in our fleet.

I've attached the sensitivity CSV and a one-page journeymap. Key asks: can your procurement team share the expected 90-day token volume distribution by model family (large context vs standard) so we can recommend reserve sizing and the burst runway?

Next steps proposal:
1) You share 90-day token mix.
2) We propose a reserve sizing (H100 slots vs A100 baseline) and a burst configuration (L4 pool) with cost delta.
3) Pilot k8s-based private routing for the first 2 weeks to validate tail latency under realistic prefix caching.

Thanks,
Ben

Ben / Irene / Samantha —

Quick technical replies to Samantha's questions:

1) Fallback fidelity (H100 -> A100 / L4):
   - Model variants: we recommend maintaining a "compatible" A100 quantized variant (8-bit/4-bit) of the primary H100 model in the catalog. For most transformer sizes we support, outputs are behaviorally similar with minor temperature-ish differences; we include deterministic post-processing to stabilize tokenization differences.
   - Automatic fallback routing uses model-compatibility metadata + per-request safety (checksum) so clients see minimal churn. We run side-by-side A/B checks for the first 48h after any fallback event.

2) KV cache warmup and burst behavior:
   - For long-prefix sessions, KV cache is the dominant factor. When a request is routed from a cold L4 to an H100 reserve, we warm the KV cache incrementally for the active conversation (we do prefix KV streaming). That means the first few tokens might incur additional micro-latency but subsequent tokens hit the warmed cache.
   - We recommend keeping a small subset of hot-slot H100s pinned for sticky customer sessions to minimize warmups under heavy tail loads.

3) Reserve sizing heuristic (proposal):
   - If 25% of traffic needs >4k contexts, size reserve H100 capacity to cover ~40% of peak long-prefix concurrency (buffer for headroom + scheduled maintenance). Use A100 to take mid-tail and L4 for baseline burst/embeddings.

I've attached a quick latency sample file from a recent Orion-like pilot. Happy to jump on a short technical sync if helpful.

—Priyom

That reduces your capex-like exposure while giving you the memory headroom for long contexts.

Operational guardrails we'll include in the deal:
- Canary policy: new fallbacks only route 5% of traffic initially with auto-rollback on a defined quality regression delta.
- Sticky hot-slot pool: 8 H100 sticky slots reserved for active long-context sessions during peak hours.
- Cost visibility: token-level chargeback + per-route latency split in the Console.
